choices: He wanted to take charge of OpenAI directly, and the other founders refused to hand him control

new.context: In early 2018, Musk reportedly proposed either taking a majority stake in OpenAI or folding it into Tesla. The other co-founders, including Sam Altman, Greg Brockman, and Ilya Sutskever, refused — they did not want one person controlling the lab. Musk left the board in February 2018, publicly citing a Tesla conflict of interest. He later sued Altman in 2024 over the lab's shift toward for-profit work.

new.question: In April 2024, Apple sent threat alerts to iPhone users in 92 countries about powerful spyware. Which Israeli firm's product was the most-named example?
new.answer: NSO Group, makers of the Pegasus spyware that targets phones of journalists and activists
choices: NSO Group, makers of the Pegasus spyware that targets phones of journalists and activists
Apple itself, which had quietly built spyware into iOS and then warned users about it
Google, which had been sold the spyware by Apple in a secret deal earlier that year
The United Nations, which runs a global phone-monitoring program from a Geneva office
new.context: Pegasus is spyware sold by Israel-based NSO Group to governments. It can silently turn on a phone's microphone and camera and read messages. Apple has sent 'mercenary spyware' alerts to users in over 150 countries since 2021, mostly targeting journalists, activists, and politicians. The April 2024 wave reached 92 countries in a single day.

new.context: Gaggle, GoGuardian, and Bark scan student email, search, and writing on school accounts for words like 'gun' or 'kill.' One Kansas district found almost two-thirds of over 1,200 alerts were false (homework, photo assignments, jokes). A student joking about guns in a school document was reported to police in one case. Critics warn students self-censor when they know everything they type is read.

new.question: Lawsuits like Murthy v. Missouri (2024) used the Twitter Files to argue what about US government and social-media platforms?
new.answer: Officials had been 'jawboning' — pressuring platforms to delete posts the First Amendment bars
choices: Officials had been 'jawboning' — pressuring platforms to delete posts the First Amendment bars
Every post needed approval — from a federal judge before it could appear online anywhere
Platforms had been translating posts — into Russian for secret review by foreign agents
Officials had been paying users — in gift cards to write supportive posts about new laws
new.context: Murthy v. Missouri reached the Supreme Court in 2024. Plaintiffs argued the federal government had pressured platforms through 'trust-and-safety' channels — informal requests with implicit consequences. The Court dismissed the case in June 2024, ruling plaintiffs lacked standing, without resolving the underlying First Amendment question. 'Jawboning' is the legal term for this kind of indirect pressure on private speech.

new.context: DHS announced the board April 27, 2022. Critics on the right called it a 'Ministry of Truth,' echoing Orwell's 1984. Jankowicz received death threats. The episode showed how quickly content-moderation infrastructure can attract bipartisan distrust depending on who runs it.

new.question: Israeli company Cellebrite sells phone-unlocking tools to police worldwide, including authoritarian countries. Why is this kind of tool worrying?
new.answer: Once a tool to break into phones exists and is sold, the buyer list is hard to control
choices: Once a tool to break into phones exists and is sold, the buyer list is hard to control
The tools only work on phones made before 2010 and cannot reach any modern devices
Cellebrite tools are required by law to be reviewed by the United Nations before any sale
Phone unlocking tools always fail on encrypted messages and are useless against any chat app
new.context: Cellebrite sells UFED kits that extract data from locked phones. Customers include US police but also Belarus, Saudi Arabia, and other governments accused of targeting dissidents. Once a capability is built and sold, it tends to spread; tools sold for one purpose under one government become available for other purposes under the next. This is a general pattern for surveillance technology.

new.question: In April 2024, President Biden signed a law called PAFACA that targeted TikTok. What did the law actually require?
new.answer: ByteDance had to sell TikTok's US business within roughly 270 days or US app stores must drop the app
choices: ByteDance had to sell TikTok's US business within roughly 270 days or US app stores must drop the app

new.context: PAFACA (Protecting Americans from Foreign Adversary Controlled Applications Act) was signed April 24, 2024. It applied to apps controlled by foreign adversaries and named TikTok's parent ByteDance specifically. Concerns centered on China's 2017 National Intelligence Law, which requires Chinese organizations to assist intelligence work. The Supreme Court upheld PAFACA in January 2025.
